issues.description: Deprecation is the right move: removing incidental complexity that duplicated stdlib.
issues.detail: The change correctly identifies that falcon.testing.redirected was incidental complexity — a thin wrapper complecting two independent concerns (stdout and stderr redirection) into one helper, when contextlib already provides the decomposed primitives. Pointing users at contextlib.redirect_stdout/redirect_stderr is the simpler-not-easier move. SIMPLE.

issues.description: Deprecation message names both replacements but elides that they are two separate context managers.
issues.detail: A caller passing both stdout and stderr to the old helper gets one with-block; the replacement requires nesting two context managers (or contextlib.ExitStack). The message says 'use X and Y' without noting they don't compose into a single call. A one-line migration example in the docstring would prevent the obvious confusion. EASY-NOT-SIMPLE for the migrator.

issues.description: Test asserts on the deprecation message string rather than the behavior contract.
issues.detail: test_deprecated_redirected matches on the exact wording 'Please use contextlib.redirect_stdout and contextlib.redirect_stderr instead.' That couples the test to prose, not to the value (a DeprecatedWarning was emitted) or the behavior (output was captured). Matching on a stable substring like 'deprecated' or just asserting the warning class would be the simpler test. TDD-AS-DESIGN, mildly.

issues.description: The question that should have been asked first: why did this helper exist at all?
issues.detail: Before deprecating, it's worth naming what redirected was solving that contextlib didn't at the time it was written — and confirming nothing downstream still relies on that. The PR asserts equivalence but doesn't show it (e.g., behavior on exceptions, nested use, generator semantics). A short note in the newsfragment about exact equivalence would close the loop.

review.summary: This is a small, correct decomplection: a helper that braided two stdlib primitives into one wrapper is being pointed back at the primitives it duplicated. The diff is clean, the deprecation machinery is consistent with the project's existing pattern (matches the httpnow deprecation), and the internal call sites are updated in the same PR. The remaining notes are minor: the deprecation message could acknowledge that the replacement is two context managers rather than one; the test over-specifies the warning's prose; and the newsfragment could briefly assert behavioral equivalence so future readers don't have to rediscover why the wrapper existed. SIMPLE overall — nothing here should block merge.
